parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State, by reference to the power dissipated in a resistor, what is meant by the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating voltage.

markscheme_points.text: peak E shown as ± 17 V or ± 24 V

hints: Hint 1: Think about comparing an alternating voltage that is always changing to a steady direct voltage - what common effect in a resistor could you use to say they are equivalent?
Hint 2: Focus on the average heating effect over a full cycle and how you would express that mean power using a steady voltage value.
parts.proper_answer: The r.m.s. value of an alternating voltage is the value of a direct voltage that dissipates the same mean power in the same resistor.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What r.m.s. Really Means**
An alternating voltage keeps changing from positive to negative, so its heating effect keeps changing too. To give it a useful single value, you compare it to a steady d.c. voltage that does the same job.

Step 2: **Linking to Power in a Resistor**
In a resistor of resistance $R$, the mean power from the alternating voltage is the same as the steady power from the equivalent d.c. voltage. That is $$P_{mean} = \frac{V_{r.m.s.}^2}{R}$$ So $V_{r.m.s.}$ is the d.c. voltage that would produce the same mean heating power in the same $R$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A coil is rotating freely, on frictionless bearings, at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field. This rotation causes an induced alternating electromotive force (e.m.f.) across the open terminals of the coil. The induced e.m.f. has r.m.s. value $12\text{ V}$ and frequency $50\text{ Hz}$.

The speed of rotation of the coil is now doubled.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State and explain, with reference to the principles of electromagnetic induction, the effect of the increased speed of rotation on the r.m.s. value of the induced e.m.f.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what actually creates the induced e.m.f. in the rotating coil - it is not the flux itself but how fast that flux through the coil is changing.
Hint 2: Think about what doubling the rotation speed does to the time taken for one cycle and therefore to the rate at which flux linkage changes.
parts.proper_answer: Rate of change of flux linkage doubles, so by Faraday's law induced e.m.f. doubles. R.m.s. e.m.f. increases from 12 V to 24 V.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Faraday's Law Governs the Size**
The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage: $$E \propto \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}$$ where $N\Phi$ is flux linkage. Faster rotation means the same flux change happens in less time.

Step 2: **Doubling the Speed**
Doubling rotation speed halves the time $\Delta t$ for a given change $\Delta(N\Phi)$, so $\Delta(N\Phi)/\Delta t$ doubles. Hence peak and r.m.s. e.m.f. both double, from $12\text{ V}$ r.m.s. to $24\text{ V}$ r.m.s.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: power as (the mean power of) the alternating voltage

hints: Hint 1: Start from the original frequency of 50 Hz and think about what doubling the coil speed does to the number of cycles per second and to the period.
Hint 2: Consider how the new r.m.s. value from (b)(i) is related to the peak value you need to draw, remembering the sine wave shape starting at zero.
Hint 3: Count how many full periods of the new faster oscillation will fit into the 0 to 20 ms window shown on Fig. 9.1.
parts.proper_answer: Sine wave from 0, with period 10 ms (2 full cycles in 20 ms) and peak about 34 V. $f = 100\text{ Hz}$, $T = 10\text{ ms}$, $E_0 = 24\sqrt{2} \approx 34\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **New Frequency and Period**
Original $f = 50\text{ Hz}$, so $$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{50} = 0.020\text{ s} = 20\text{ ms}$$ Doubling speed doubles $f$ to $100\text{ Hz}$. So $$T_{new} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.010\text{ s} = 10\text{ ms}$$ In $20\text{ ms}$ you will see two complete cycles.

Step 2: **New Peak Value**
For a sinusoid, peak and r.m.s. are linked by $$E_0 = \sqrt{2} \times E_{r.m.s.}$$ With $E_{r.m.s.} = 24\text{ V}$: $$E_0 = 24 \times \sqrt{2} \approx 34\text{ V}$$

Step 3: **Shape to Sketch**
Draw a sine wave starting at $E = 0$ at $t = 0$ going positive first, reaching about $+34\text{ V}$ near $2.5\text{ ms}$, back to zero at $5\text{ ms}$, to $-34\text{ V}$ near $7.5\text{ ms}$, to zero at $10\text{ ms}$, then repeat identically from $10$ to $20\text{ ms}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the motion of the coil in (b) of connecting a load resistor across its terminals.

markscheme_points.text: force on wire is upwards, so reading decreases (becomes perpendicular to the field)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is different when the terminals are connected - can a current now flow and where does the power dissipated in that resistor have to come from?
Hint 2: Recall Lenz's law about the direction of induced effects and what that implies for the forces on the current-carrying coil sides in the magnetic field.
parts.proper_answer: Coil slows down and stops. Current dissipates power in resistor, energy taken from rotational kinetic energy of coil, with induced forces opposing the rotation by Lenz's law.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Current Now Flows and Power is Needed**
With open terminals no current flows. Connecting a load lets the induced e.m.f. drive a current, so mean power $$P = \frac{V_{r.m.s.}^2}{R}$$ is dissipated as heat in the resistor. By conservation of energy this cannot come from nothing.

Step 2: **Electromagnetic Braking**
The energy comes from the rotational kinetic energy of the coil. By Lenz's law the induced current creates forces that oppose the motion producing it. With no external drive and frictionless bearings, this braking torque slows the coil until it stops.
